---
title: "Quiz: fitting a mixture with EM"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. E-step: responsibilities $r_{ik}$; M-step: $N_k = \sum_i r_{ik}$, $\pi_k = N_k/n$, weighted means and covariances.

---

**Q1.** In one sentence each: what does the E-step compute, and what does the M-step compute?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One step uses the parameters to get labels, the other the labels to get parameters.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
E-step: with the current parameters, the responsibility of every component for every point (soft labels, by Bayes' rule). M-step: with these responsibilities as weights, new weights $\pi_k$, means and covariances (a weighted fit of each Gaussian).
:::

---

**Q2.** Three points $x = 0, 1, 10$ have responsibilities $r_{i1} = 1, 0.5, 0$ for component 1. What are $N_1$, $\mu_1$ and $\pi_1$ after the M-step?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Weighted mean with weights $r_{i1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$N_1 = 1.5$, $\mu_1 = (1 \cdot 0 + 0.5 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 10)/1.5 = 0.33$, $\pi_1 = 1.5/3 = 0.5$.
:::

---

**Q3.** What do you have to change in EM to get exactly k-means?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Labels, covariances, weights.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Make the labels hard (each point fully to its nearest centre), give every component the same round covariance $\sigma^2 I$ (not re-estimated) and equal weights (not re-estimated). Equivalently: equal round covariances with $\sigma \to 0$, where the soft responsibilities become 0 or 1 by themselves.
:::

---

**Q4.** The log-likelihood plot of your EM run shows a drop between two iterations. What can you conclude?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the theory say about EM's log-likelihood?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Something is not plain EM: a bug, a numerical problem (for instance a variance clipped at a floor in a way the M-step does not account for), or a modified algorithm (hard assignments, fixed weights). Exact EM never decreases the log-likelihood.
:::

---

**Q5.** Two runs of EM on the same data end with log-likelihoods −1520 and −1384. Which do you keep, and why can this happen?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Local maxima.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Keep the run with −1384 (higher likelihood). EM only finds a local maximum, which depends on the start; the other run got stuck, for example with two components sharing one group.
:::

---

**Q6.** One component of your fit has a variance of $10^{-9}$ and sits on a single pixel value, and the log-likelihood is huge. What happened, and how do you prevent it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the density of a Gaussian at its centre when σ → 0?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The component collapsed onto one data point: its density there grows like $1/\sigma$, so the likelihood is unbounded, although the fit is useless. Prevent it with a variance floor (add $\varepsilon$ to every variance), by restarting collapsed components, or with a prior on the covariances. Many identical values (e.g. saturated pixels) make it especially likely.
:::

---

**Q7.** Adding a fourth component raises $\log p(\mathcal D)$ from −2050 to −2046 on $n = 500$ points; it adds 6 parameters. Does BIC accept it? Does AIC?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare $2 \times$ the gain in log-likelihood with $p\ln n$ and with $2p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$-2\log p$ drops by 8. BIC adds $6\ln 500 = 37.3$: worse by 29.3, rejected. AIC adds 12: worse by 4, also rejected. (With a gain of 10 in $\log p$, i.e. 20 in $-2\log p$, AIC would accept and BIC still reject.)
:::

---

**Q8.** Why is the log-likelihood alone useless for choosing the number of components?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens with one component per point?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
More components (or more flexible covariances) can only fit the same data at least as well, so the maximum likelihood never decreases with $K$; with one component per point it is even infinite. A penalty for the number of parameters (BIC, AIC), or a test on held-out data, is needed.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that for any distribution $q(k)$ over the components, $\log p(\mathbf x) \ge \sum_k q(k)\log\frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)}{q(k)}$, with equality when $q(k) = r_k(\mathbf x)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Jensen's inequality for the concave $\log$: $\log E[Y] \ge E[\log Y]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\log p(\mathbf x) = \log\sum_k q(k)\,\frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)}{q(k)} = \log E_q[Y] \ge E_q[\log Y]$ with $Y = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)/q(k)$. For $q(k) = r_k(\mathbf x) = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)/p(\mathbf x)$, $Y = p(\mathbf x)$ for every $k$: a constant, so both sides equal $\log p(\mathbf x)$.
:::
